title: Hedge Funds Slashed Jobs and Dumped Trades After Market's Thursday Rout
detail:
Hedge Funds Slashed Jobs and Dumped Trades After Market's Thursday Rout
Matias Civita
Fri, November 6, 2026 at 1:46 PM MST 3 min read
^GSPC
^IXIC
Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images

Hedge funds are cutting investment teams and abandoning trades after October's market rout inflicted losses across the industry, with Thursday's technology selloff deepening a retreat that had already erased substantial gains, The Wall Street Journal reported.

The pressure extends from funds investing in artificial intelligence and healthcare stocks to firms trading risky corporate debt. Managers are shrinking businesses, reducing borrowed money and, in some cases, preparing to return capital to investors.

Stock-picking hedge funds unwound positions in October at the fastest pace in more than a decade, according to a Morgan Stanley client note cited by the Journal. Their market exposure has fallen about 9% since June.

More than 40% of those funds were flat or losing money for the year through October, Morgan Stanley said, even as the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite remained positive for 2026.

The widening damage is reshaping some prominent firms. Samlyn Capital, which manages approximately $7 billion, is concentrating on financial-services stocks, prompting departures among investment employees and leaders covering other sectors, the Journal reported, citing people familiar with the firm. Its fund lost about 5% through October.

Engineers Gate, a roughly $4 billion firm launched by Glenn Dubin, is closing most of its "quantamental" business, which blends human investment judgment with quantitative methods. All but five portfolio managers in that strategy are being cut, and business head Mike Daylamani is leaving, according to the report.

The firm, run by co-founder Greg Eisner, remains focused on quantitative investing. It was down in the mid-single digits through October, the Journal reported. Bloomberg previously reported staff reductions there.

At Lone Pine Capital, the reversal has been especially severe. Its hedge fund gained more than 40% during the first half before enduring its worst quarterly stretch in the third quarter, according to a person familiar with the firm cited by the Journal.

An additional 8.8% loss before fees in October left the fund down 7.5% before fees for the year. Lone Pine managed about $19 billion as of September. The firm's investor letter attributed the damage to falling AI stocks and unsuccessful bets against companies it considered threatened by the technology.

Those companies' shares rose instead, hurting positions intended to profit from declines. Thursday brought another blow. Funds focused on telecommunications, media and technology lost more than 4%, Goldman Sachs told clients, essentially wiping out annual gains that had reached as much as 24% before the summer AI retreat.

title: Stocks See Slight Rebound After Thursday's Rout But Remain Well Below Highs

Stocks See Slight Rebound After Thursday's Rout But Remain Well Below Highs
Demian Bio

^IXIC
^DJI
^GSPC
MU
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Stocks climbed on Monday as investors bought the dip following a string of losses.Getty Images

Stocks attempted a rebound on Friday after a brutal selloff on Thursday, in which the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite saw its worst session in over a year and a half.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average edged down, dropping 0.46%, while the S&P 500 gained 0.32% and the Nasdaq Composite did so 1.09%.

Shares of technological companies saw gains but were small when compared to Thursday's plunge. Micron climbed 5% but plummeted 17% on Thursday. Nvidia also gained almost 3% after falling 9%.

The tech-heavy index entered correction territory after Thursday, finishing more than 11% below its October record. The retreat crossed Wall Street's correction threshold, a decline of at least 10% from a recent peak. A drop of 20% marks a bear market.

For investors wondering what comes next, past corrections offer reasons for patience, but little assurance that the worst is already over.

A CNBC analysis of 10 previous Nasdaq corrections over the past decade found that several episodes brought additional losses during the following month. Corrections in 2025, 2022, 2020 and 2018 all featured further selling over that period.

Yet the picture generally improved over longer stretches. Among those episodes, the index had returned to gains after six months in every case except 2022, according to the analysis. Across the historical sample, there were average gains of 9.41% over three months and 17.03% over six months from correction bottoms.

The jobs report also dominated the news after blowing past expectations. Nonfarm payrolls climbed by a seasonally adjusted 165,000 last month, way above the 59,000 expected by the Dow Jones consensus.

At the same time, the unemployment rate fell to 4.1%, lower than the 4.2% expected by analysts.

Previous months were also revised to the upside. August added more than 50,000 additional extra jobs, while September gained 31,000 more than originally reported.

Payroll gains were also better than expected, with average hourly gains climbing 0.4% last month and 3.1% for the year, compared to 0.3% and 2.9%, respectively.

Private sector figures also surprised to the upside earlier this week. ADP showed that companies added 86,000 jobs, compared to the 75,000 expected by the Dow Jones consensus.

ADP said that "hiring showed solid growth for a second month and pay gains were steady," but noted there were "weak spots," as "professional and business services lost jobs for the third straight month."

"Employers of all sizes were hiring last month, and our data suggests that job-changers were lured by a combination of bonuses, overtime, and more hours in addition to higher base pay. Taken together, earnings growth for these workers hit its fastest pace since March 2024," said Dr. Nela Richardson, ADP's Chief Economist.

Trade, transportation and utilities gained some 39,000 new roles. Education and health services kept hiring, with 28,000 jobs, while leisure and hospitality gained 19,000. In contrast, professional and business services shed 27,000 positions. Natural resources and mining lost 8,000.

title: Stocks rebound after tech selloff that pushed Nasdaq into correction
detail:
Stocks rebound after tech selloff that pushed Nasdaq into correction
Mary Cunningham
Fri, November 6, 2026 at 12:06 PM MST 3 min read
^GSPC
^DJI
^IXIC

Stocks showed signs of life as U.S. financial markets opened on Friday, stabilizing after a steep selloff the previous day driven by concerns over a potential slowdown in data center construction.

The S&P 500 rose 31 points, or 0.5%, in afternoon trading, failing to erase the sharp losses it suffered Thursday on its worst day since April 2025. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite rose 259 points, or 1.1%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was flat.

Financial markets soared immediately after the midterm elections earlier this week, but quickly reversed course on Thursday as investors assessed whether sweeping Democratic victories could lead to tighter restrictions on building data centers and weaker spending on artificial intelligence.

Although Democrats will control both the House and Senate when newly elected lawmakers take office in January, President Trump will retain veto authority, which will likely limit the passage of major restrictions on data centers. Opposition is more likely to surface at the state and local level, Wall Street analysts said.

As of Friday, voters had approved more than 40 ballot measures restricting data centers in communities across the country, according to an analysis from political research firm Redbud Consulting.

Tech stocks started to recover on Friday, helping pull the Nasdaq higher after a brutal beating on Thursday that caused the index to shed more than 1,400 points and enter a "correction," or when stocks fall at least 10% from their previous peak.

Chipmaker Nvidia — a bellwether for the AI sector — gained 2.5% in afternoon trading, and semiconductor manufacturer Micron Technology rose 3.9%. The so-called hyperscalers — the companies leading the data center buildout — saw modest gains, with Google-owner Alphabet climbing 0.8%, Amazon up 0.9% and Meta gaining 2.1%; Microsoft shed 0.6%.

IREN, a company that delivers data centers, compute and software for AI training, reported stronger-than-expected results for its latest quarter. Its stock jumped 19.2%, and it also announced two new contracts signed since the end of the quarter.

"We own the land, the power and the data centers under all of it, which gives us more ways to fund growth and lets us set its pace," co-CEO Daniel Roberts said.

Outside of AI, markets were mixed, and more S&P 500 stocks fell than rose.

Slowing AI investment?

A key question for Wall Street is whether AI companies will deliver the revenue growth investors are banking on. Anthropic, which filed for an initial public offering last month and is expected to debut on the Nasdaq this month, will serve as a critical test case. While filing highlighted rapid growth, the company has yet to turn a profit.
